paragraphs: A forecasting model can make large errors because it is weak or because the particular signal is difficult to predict. This paper develops an evaluation framework that helps separate those explanations. Its goal is to make benchmark results more informative than a single average error or leaderboard position.

The framework introduces Spectral Coherence Predictability, or SCP, as an efficiently computed difficulty reference for individual forecasting instances. It also derives a corresponding lower bound on linear forecasting error. A second measure, the Linear Utilization Ratio, describes how effectively a model uses linearly predictable information across different frequencies. These measures connect performance to the structure available in the data.

On synthetic and real datasets, SCP strongly tracks observed errors across the evaluated forecasters. The analysis also finds that predictability changes over time and across variables. Grouping results by difficulty and frequency reveals complementary architectural strengths. These findings support comparisons that account for changing task difficulty, while keeping the framework’s linear predictability reference distinct from a universal limit on forecasting.
icml-2026-beyond-model-ranking-predictab.tldr: The paper evaluates forecasting models against instance-level predictability to reveal strengths and weaknesses hidden by aggregate rankings.

paragraphs: Reconstructing RAW sensor data from a processed RGB image requires working backward through transformations that have already discarded information. The paper addresses this inherently ambiguous reconstruction problem. It targets a trade-off in existing methods: generative approaches can produce high-quality results but cost substantial computation, while fast regression methods can smooth away detail and depart from authentic sensor signals.

SHADE uses a deterministic flow that produces a reconstruction in one step. The authors report that this approach captures broader transport patterns between the image representations, rather than relying on point-to-point regression alone. Their analysis also supports robustness to perturbations in the input. A second component aligns representations using a student–teacher DINO pair initialized homogeneously, so both sides work within a shared feature space.

Experiments report state-of-the-art reconstruction performance across multiple benchmarks. The contribution is a combination of efficient generation and feature alignment intended to improve fidelity. Because the original processing loses information irreversibly, these results concern reconstruction quality rather than guaranteed recovery of the exact original sensor measurements.
icml-2026-bridging-rgb-and-raw-single-st.tldr: SHADE combines a one-step deterministic flow with shared-space feature alignment for accurate, efficient reconstruction of RAW data from RGB images.

paragraphs: A spoken dialogue system can fail early if an unfamiliar accent causes it to identify the wrong language. That mistake can then disrupt later dialogue processing. This paper targets language detection when dialects and accents are underrepresented and training data are scarce, a setting where conventional fine-tuning can be expensive and prone to overfitting.

The proposed Convex Language Detection framework places a convex optimization objective inside the speech processing pipeline. Its implementation uses the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers in JAX across multiple GPUs. The authors establish global optimality guarantees and polynomial-time training for the formulation. They also prove stability properties for its decision margins and provide guarantees concerning perturbations to input features.

The experiments report 97–98% accuracy in challenging low-resource settings, alongside sample efficiency and robustness to dialect variation. These results connect the mathematical formulation to a practical failure point in speech systems. The theoretical guarantees concern the proposed objective and feature perturbations; the reported accuracy is empirical evidence from the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-convex-low-resource-accent-rob.tldr: CLD uses convex optimization to improve language detection under limited data and accent variation, with theoretical stability guarantees and reported accuracy of 97–98%.

paragraphs: Aligning language models with human preferences can require substantial computation and complicated training procedures. Direct Preference Optimization simplifies some of this work, but the paper identifies remaining problems with ranking consistency, GPU demand, and tuning cost. COALA proposes a lighter preference-learning approach built around a convex reformulation of neural networks.

The method removes the need for a reference model and reduces both training time and GPU memory use, enabling training on a single GPU. Its convex optimization foundation also provides theoretical guarantees. The practical aim is to make preference fine-tuning less resource intensive while retaining competitive alignment performance.

The authors evaluate six models on four datasets, including a synthetic educational feedback dataset with 26,621 samples. COALA uses as little as approximately 17.6% of DPO’s total floating-point computation in the reported experiments. It also shows steadily increasing rewards and reaches peak margins sooner than DPO and ORPO. These findings support an efficiency advantage in the tested settings, alongside competitive performance rather than a claim of uniformly superior accuracy.
icml-2026-convex-optimization-for-alignm.tldr: COALA applies convex optimization to preference fine-tuning, enabling single-GPU training with competitive performance and substantially reduced computation.

paragraphs: During long-sequence inference, a transformer’s stored keys and values can consume substantial memory. Removing cache entries reduces this burden, but can change the model’s attention outputs. This paper studies which entries matter by analyzing those output changes directly, giving cache eviction a formal basis beyond selecting entries using attention weights alone.

The analysis finds that an entry’s importance also depends on its value state and the model’s pretrained parameter matrices. CriticalKV uses these factors in a selection algorithm that optimizes worst-case output perturbation under a perturbation constraint. The algorithm is designed to augment existing eviction methods with negligible additional computational overhead.

Across three language models, three existing eviction methods, and 29 datasets from Ruler and LongBench, the enhancement reduces the performance loss caused by compression by more than half on average. Further analysis at attention-head and layer levels supports the proposed explanation. The result concerns preserving model behavior under cache compression: it does not mean that memory use or total inference time is halved.
icml-2026-criticalkv-optimizing-kv-cache.tldr: CriticalKV selects cache entries by their potential effect on attention outputs, cutting compression-related performance loss by more than half on average in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models increase available model capacity while activating only selected experts for each input. Making experts smaller and more numerous can create additional combinations, but also increases routing overhead. This paper explores another way to improve such models: changing how the selected experts’ outputs are assembled.

Standard aggregation combines expert outputs through a weighted sum. The authors theoretically show that structural aggregation can expand the space of expert combinations without changing the experts or router. They also argue that it makes multi-step reasoning within one mixture-of-experts layer possible. DAG-MoE implements this idea through a lightweight module that learns the aggregation structure among selected experts.

Experiments in standard language modeling settings show consistent improvements over traditional mixture-of-experts baselines during both pretraining and fine-tuning. The findings identify aggregation as a useful additional design choice for scaling performance. The possibility of multi-step reasoning is part of the structural argument; the reported empirical result is improved language modeling performance, rather than direct proof that every layer performs such reasoning.
icml-2026-dag-moe-from-simple-mixture-to.tldr: DAG-MoE learns structured combinations of expert outputs, expanding their possible interactions and improving reported pretraining and fine-tuning performance.

paragraphs: A long video can be mostly authentic while containing a small manipulated segment. Analyzing isolated short clips does not fully capture this setting. The paper defines a task that asks a forensic system to determine authenticity, locate manipulated intervals in time, and explain the evidence for those judgments within an untrimmed video.

To support this task, the authors introduce TASLE, a benchmark containing 12,472 long, untrimmed videos with varied manipulation patterns. Its annotations include authenticity labels, temporal boundaries, and explanations for individual segments. This combination supports evaluation of where a manipulation occurs as well as the reasoning attached to its detection.

The proposed baseline, MSLoc, first scans the video with a boundary-sensitive proposal module. A multimodal large language model then refines the proposed boundaries and supplies interpretable reasoning. This coarse-to-fine organization combines efficient scanning with closer inspection of candidate segments. The experiments support the baseline’s effectiveness and the value of evaluating localized, explainable forensics in long videos. The abstract states that the dataset and code will be released.
icml-2026-explainable-forensics-of-manip.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark and coarse-to-fine system for locating and explaining AI-manipulated segments within otherwise authentic long videos.

paragraphs: Agents can reuse past interactions to improve planning and reasoning, but retrieving those experiences as text adds tokens and separates retrieval from generation. ExpWeaver instead stores and accesses experience through the language model’s internal representations. This brings experience retrieval into the generation process without requiring a separate retrieval-augmented generation module.

The system encodes experiences using the model’s hidden states and retrieves relevant representations at each decoding step. Cross-attention combines the retrieved information, while a gated residual mechanism controls its integration. Reinforcement learning trains the pipeline end to end for both generating outputs and ranking candidates.

Across 13 tasks, the authors report state-of-the-art results on 12 and an improvement of over 6.8% against the strongest baseline. Token use remains comparable to systems without retrieval, while text-based retrieval methods use 1.5–2 times as many tokens. Transfer experiments report improvements of 16.32% with no target-domain examples and 15.21% with a few examples. Together, these results support experience reuse that improves the evaluated tasks without the token expansion associated with inserting retrieved text.
icml-2026-expweaver-llm-agents-learn-fro.tldr: ExpWeaver retrieves past experience through internal model representations, improving reported task performance while keeping token use comparable to non-retrieval baselines.

paragraphs: SAM3D reconstructs three-dimensional content from images, but its inference latency makes deployment difficult. This paper investigates why generic acceleration methods are unreliable in that pipeline. It identifies different computational needs across shape and layout generation, sparse texture refinement, and geometries with different spectral characteristics.

Fast-SAM3D responds with three mechanisms that allocate computation according to current generation complexity. Modality-aware caching treats structural changes separately from sensitive layout updates. Joint spatial and temporal token selection concentrates refinement on high-entropy regions. Spectral-aware token aggregation changes decoding resolution to account for differences across geometries. These components target distinct sources of uneven computational demand.

The framework requires no additional training. Experiments report end-to-end speedups of up to 2.67 times with negligible loss of fidelity, improving the observed trade-off between reconstruction quality and runtime. The broader contribution is evidence that acceleration benefits from respecting the internal differences within a generation pipeline. Its reported speedup is an experimental maximum, and negligible fidelity loss does not imply perfectly identical reconstructions.
icml-2026-fast-sam3d-3dfy-anything-in-im.tldr: Fast-SAM3D adapts caching, refinement, and decoding to different generation demands, achieving up to 2.67× speedup without additional training.

paragraphs: Domain incremental learning asks a model to adapt as new data domains arrive without retraining from scratch. Changes between domains can sharply reduce performance and interfere with previously learned behavior. HEDP addresses this setting with a prompt-based framework that combines two kinds of evidence when selecting a domain.

Inspired by Helmholtz free energy, the method adds an energy regularization loss that encourages domain representations to be easier to distinguish. It then combines energy-based information with distance-based information through a weighted mechanism. The two components serve related purposes: learning more separable representations and using both cues to improve domain selection and generalization.

Experiments on multiple benchmarks, including CORe50, report stronger performance on unseen domains and a 2.57% accuracy improvement. The results also support reduced catastrophic forgetting and better adaptability to new domains. The significance is that distinguishing known domain representations can be paired with a more informative selection mechanism to support continued adaptation. The reported outcome is mitigation of forgetting, rather than a claim that earlier knowledge is always preserved completely.
icml-2026-hedp-a-hybrid-energy-distance-.tldr: HEDP combines energy and distance cues in a prompt-based framework to improve domain adaptation and reduce forgetting.

paragraphs: A universal robot controller must handle robots with different body structures, but transformer-based controllers can be costly to deploy. Existing approaches also have limited ability to transfer between tasks. DivMorph addresses both problems by training controllers whose knowledge can be separated into reusable and specialized components.

The method first factorizes randomly initialized transformer weights using singular value decomposition, producing basic knowledge units. During training, soft gates conditioned on the task and robot morphology modulate those units. This process develops shared components called learngenes and specialized components called tailors. The controller can then be recomposed by activating the components relevant to a particular robot and task.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, a 3.3-fold improvement in sample efficiency for cross-task transfer, and a 16.7-fold reduction in model size for deploying a single agent. The two efficiency results address different needs: learning new tasks with fewer samples and deploying a smaller controller. They support the value of decomposable knowledge without implying that the reported model-size reduction is itself an equivalent runtime speedup.
icml-2026-knowledge-diversion-for-effici.tldr: DivMorph separates shared and specialized controller knowledge to improve robot policy transfer and substantially reduce single-agent deployment size.

paragraphs: LoRA reduces fine-tuning cost by allowing weight updates only within a small, low-rank subspace. That restriction makes the initial choice of directions consequential: limited adaptation capacity can be spent on directions that matter little for the target task. This paper examines how to choose those directions using downstream data.

The authors argue that properties of pretrained weights alone do not adequately describe task relevance. Their Fisher-guided framework instead uses curvature information induced by the target data distribution to characterize how parameter changes affect model predictions. This supplies a task-dependent criterion for selecting the subspace in which LoRA will learn.

Experiments across varied tasks and modalities show consistent, significant downstream improvements over existing initialization approaches. The findings support treating initialization as an informed allocation of adaptation capacity, using the model’s interaction with target data to guide that allocation. The contribution is specifically a better starting subspace for low-rank fine-tuning, with empirical evidence that data-aware sensitivity is more useful than relying only on pretrained weight geometry.
icml-2026-learning-in-the-fisher-subspac.tldr: The paper initializes LoRA using target-data Fisher information to select adaptation directions that better affect task-relevant predictions.

paragraphs: Alzheimer’s disease changes electrical brain activity and coordination across EEG channels. Many classifiers predict disease status without explicitly describing the event timing or channel relationships behind their decisions. LERD models those hidden dynamics directly, aiming to combine useful classification with summaries that relate to brain physiology.

The system learns latent neural events and their relationships from multichannel EEG without annotations identifying events or interactions. It combines continuous-time event inference with a stochastic process for generating events, allowing flexible timing patterns. An electrophysiology-inspired dynamical prior guides learning. The theoretical analysis provides a tractable regularizer based on an initial-value problem and guarantees concerning stability of the inferred relational dynamics.

On synthetic benchmarks and two real Alzheimer’s EEG cohorts, LERD consistently outperforms the strong baselines evaluated by the authors. It also produces summaries of event rates, timing, and relational graphs that align with physiology and help describe group-level differences. These findings support interpreting classification through learned dynamics, while the stated physiological summaries concern differences between groups.
icml-2026-lerd-latent-event-relational-d.tldr: LERD learns hidden EEG events and channel relationships to improve Alzheimer’s classification while producing physiology-aligned summaries of group differences.

paragraphs: Preference alignment often depends on desirable response examples that are costly to collect and use in training. This paper investigates another route: reducing the influence of undesirable examples through machine unlearning. Its central question is how to decide which negative examples are worth targeting when the goal is better alignment.

The authors develop a quantitative connection between unlearning and preference alignment through bi-level optimization. This formulation evaluates how unlearning particular negative examples changes alignment performance. The analysis finds substantial variation between examples, meaning that negative examples do not all provide the same opportunity for improvement.

Unlearning to Align, or U2A, builds on that observation by selecting and weighting examples through the bi-level framework before unlearning them. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is therefore both an analysis of example-specific effects and a procedure for using those effects to guide training. It treats negative-example selection as an optimization problem, rather than assuming that removing the influence of any undesirable example will help alignment equally.
icml-2026-leveraging-machine-unlearning-.tldr: U2A selects and weights negative examples for unlearning according to their estimated effect on preference alignment.

paragraphs: Transferable adversarial prompts allow researchers to test black-box language models using attacks developed against accessible surrogate models. Optimizing across several surrogates seems promising, but standard methods have produced only modest benefits. This paper attributes that weakness to unstable optimization when gradients from different models are combined.

Lookahead-GCG applies a stochastic Nesterov optimization approach to reduce sensitivity to individual gradient updates. It combines this with momentum represented in embedding space, enabling the approach to work with discrete prompt tokens. A further initialization strategy is intended to take advantage of the resulting generalization. Together, these components target the optimization difficulties of training against multiple models.

The reported experiments achieve attack success rates of 50.37% on open-source models and 34.03% on closed-source models. The authors report stronger results than GCG and TransferAttack, with a +11.78% gain from multi-model optimization. These results support the claim that the optimizer can affect attack transferability. They are measurements of adversarial robustness in the evaluated settings, rather than guarantees that a prompt transfers successfully to every model.
icml-2026-lookahead-gcg-improving-univer.tldr: Lookahead-GCG improves reported jailbreak transferability by stabilizing adversarial prompt optimization across multiple surrogate models.

paragraphs: Different sensing modalities provide complementary information, but they do not necessarily learn well under one shared optimization process. The paper identifies entangled updates and a uniform learning pace as obstacles to balanced multimodal learning. MoNet restructures training into nested processes so that learning within modalities and combining them can be handled separately.

At the outer level, a Decoupled Multimodal Stable Memory block creates independent optimization streams for extracting semantic information across modalities. At the inner level, an Adaptive Multimodal Coordinated Fusion block attempts to integrate that information through nested memories operating at multiple timescales. The design pairs separation during learning with coordination during fusion.

Experiments on eight datasets covering three tasks show superior performance for MoNet in the reported comparisons. These findings support changing the organization of multimodal optimization, in addition to adjusting gradients or alleviating conflicts inside a single training process. The architecture’s intended benefit is to let modalities develop useful information through independent streams while still bringing those contributions together in a balanced way.
icml-2026-multimodal-nested-learning-for.tldr: MoNet separates modality-specific learning into independent streams and coordinates their fusion through nested memories operating at different timescales.

paragraphs: Generative policies can represent complex behaviors in offline reinforcement learning, but their speed and performance can pull in different directions. Iterative diffusion policies are expensive, while faster single-step consistency policies can lose performance. This paper seeks a broader formulation that moves beyond choosing between those individual model families.

The authors view diffusion, flow matching, and consistency models as ways of learning a continuous-time generative trajectory described by an ordinary differential equation. Generative Trajectory Policies, or GTPs, extend this perspective by learning the equation’s entire solution map. The paper also introduces two theoretically motivated adaptations to make the framework practical for offline reinforcement learning.

On D4RL benchmarks, GTP achieves reported state-of-the-art performance and significantly exceeds prior generative policies. It obtains perfect scores on several difficult AntMaze tasks. These results support the usefulness of the broader generative formulation for policy learning. The perfect scores apply to the specified benchmark tasks, while the conceptual contribution is a shared design framework for policy families previously treated as separate alternatives.
icml-2026-offline-reinforcement-learning.tldr: GTP unifies generative policies through continuous-time dynamics and learns their solution map, achieving reported state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning performance.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models can support robotic manipulation, but processing many visual tokens makes real-time use expensive. Simply discarding tokens can remove small geometric details, including contact points that matter for an action. This paper approaches compression as continuous resampling of visual information inside the vision encoder.

The Differentiable Grid Sampler, or GridS, predicts a small set of task-relevant coordinates and extracts their features through differentiable interpolation. This lets the module gather information at selected spatial locations instead of relying only on keeping or deleting existing tokens. Its purpose is to preserve essential geometry while reducing the visual representation to fewer than 10% of the original tokens.

Experiments on LIBERO and a real robotic platform report a 76% reduction in floating-point operations without a reduction in task success rate. These findings support geometry-aware resampling as a way to compress the visual input aggressively while retaining useful action information. The reported efficiency measure is computational work, and the unchanged success rate is an empirical result from the evaluated tasks.
icml-2026-see-what-matters-differentiabl.tldr: GridS continuously resamples task-relevant visual features, using fewer than 10% of visual tokens with a reported 76% FLOP reduction and unchanged success rate.

paragraphs: Social bias can enter a language model’s reasoning and influence the steps that follow. This paper focuses on interrupting that propagation after it begins. Self-Debias trains a model to revise biased reasoning progressively, aiming to preserve useful context while changing the continuation responsible for carrying bias forward.

The framework treats output probability as a limited resource that can be redistributed from biased shortcuts toward unbiased reasoning paths. It uses a fine-grained objective over reasoning trajectories, subject to dynamic debiasing constraints. This supports selective revision of biased suffixes while retaining valid prefixes. An online self-improvement component also generates supervision signals and filters them for consistency.

Using 20,000 annotated samples, the authors report stronger debiasing performance while preserving general reasoning capabilities. They also report self-correction without continuous external oversight. The contribution is a targeted training approach for changing how bias develops within reasoning, rather than applying only broad penalties to outputs. These findings establish reported improvements in debiasing and retained reasoning ability, without implying that every form of social bias has been eliminated.
icml-2026-self-correcting-for-debiasing-.tldr: Self-Debias trains language models to revise biased reasoning continuations while preserving valid context and general reasoning ability.

paragraphs: Agents often solve complex tasks by combining reusable skills. This modular design also creates a security risk when a skill’s implementation contains concealed malicious behavior. SkillTrojan studies backdoors placed in those implementations, showing how an agent’s ordinary composition of skills can become part of an attack.

At a high level, the attack distributes an encrypted payload across plausible-looking skill invocations and activates under a predefined trigger. The paper also describes automated creation of backdoored skills from templates and introduces a dataset of more than 3,000 curated examples. The evaluation measures both attack success and how well the agent continues to perform benign tasks.

In a representative code-based agent setting, the attacks can be highly effective while causing little degradation in ordinary behavior. On EHR SQL with GPT-5.2-1211-Global, the authors report attack success of up to 97.2% while maintaining 89.3% clean accuracy. These results expose why benign-task performance alone may miss skill-level compromise and motivate defenses that examine how skills compose and execute.
icml-2026-skilltrojan-backdoor-attacks-o.tldr: SkillTrojan demonstrates that backdoored skill implementations can compromise agents through normal skill composition while largely preserving benign-task performance.

paragraphs: Operational monitoring produces time series that can contain many zeros, abrupt changes, and substantial randomness with little temporal structure. Public datasets underrepresent these signals, partly because of proprietary restrictions and privacy concerns. This paper introduces TelecomTS to support evaluation on the kinds of data generated by a complex operational system.

Derived from a 5G telecommunications network, TelecomTS includes heterogeneous covariates with meaningful identities and explicit absolute scales. It supports anomaly detection, root cause analysis, and question answering that combines language with time series. Preserving scale addresses a problem with normalized datasets: they can remove information useful for interpreting operational measurements.

Benchmarking time series, language, reasoning, and multimodal foundation models reveals difficulty handling the dataset’s noisy, abrupt, high-variance behavior. The experiments also show the importance of retaining absolute scale. The dataset therefore contributes both a testing resource and evidence about a modeling need: observability models should be able to use measurement scale directly when it carries information relevant to practical monitoring tasks.
icml-2026-telecomts-a-multi-modal-observ.tldr: TelecomTS benchmarks operational time series and language tasks using 5G network data that preserves meaningful covariates and absolute measurement scales.

paragraphs: Adam is widely used to train neural networks, and its descent–ascent counterpart is also used when two objectives oppose each other in a zero-sum game. The paper investigates this Adam-DA optimizer theoretically. Its motivation is that practical popularity has outpaced a rigorous understanding of how the optimizer behaves in competitive learning.

The authors derive ordinary differential equations that describe continuous-time limits of Adam-DA and closely approximate its discrete updates. This creates a tractable way to study local convergence and implicit gradient regularization. The analysis finds that the roles of the first- and second-order momentum parameters are reversed relative to their established effects in minimization problems.

Experiments with generative adversarial networks across multiple architectures and datasets support the theoretical predictions. The findings matter because intuitions about momentum from ordinary minimization may point in the wrong direction for descent–ascent optimization. The paper’s evidence links its local dynamical analysis to practical adversarial training, while keeping the continuous-time equations as approximations of the discrete optimizer.
icml-2026-understanding-dynamics-of-adam.tldr: An ODE analysis of Adam-DA finds momentum effects opposite to those in minimization, with supporting experiments in adversarial network training.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate solutions to combinatorial optimization problems, but many such solvers require large training collections of near-optimal answers. This paper develops an unsupervised alternative. It adapts trajectory optimization ideas to discrete problems so that a solver can receive useful learning signals along its generative process.

The authors formulate discrete diffusion as a stochastic control problem over continuous-time Markov chains. They introduce discrete adjoint dynamics to propagate optimization information through generated trajectories. Combinatorial Adjoint Matching, or CAM, uses this formulation to provide structured, low-variance signals for training the diffusion solver at the trajectory level.

Across diverse combinatorial problems, CAM consistently outperforms the evaluated unsupervised diffusion baselines. It also achieves performance competitive with strong supervised diffusion methods and even traditional solvers. The significance is that learning without near-optimal solution labels can still produce competitive solvers when training signals account for the discrete generation trajectory. The reported comparison is competitive performance across the tested problems, rather than a guarantee of optimal solutions or universal superiority over traditional algorithms.
icml-2026-unsupervised-diffusion-solver-.tldr: CAM trains discrete diffusion solvers without solution labels by propagating structured optimization signals through their generative trajectories.

paragraphs: Long reasoning traces consume substantial computation, but length alone may say little about whether the reasoning is productive. This paper evaluates ten reasoning models on mathematical and scientific tasks. It finds that naively longer traces and more review behavior are associated with lower accuracy in the studied settings.

The authors represent reasoning as a graph and measure the Failed-Step Fraction: the share of steps belonging to branches that are later abandoned. This statistic predicts correctness more consistently than trace length or review ratio across models. It distinguishes structural failure within the reasoning process from the amount of text produced.

Two interventions probe whether this structure is practically useful. Ranking candidate traces by Failed-Step Fraction produces the largest gains in first-answer success among the compared metrics. Editing traces to remove failed branches also significantly improves accuracy, supporting the interpretation that abandoned paths can bias later reasoning. These results favor structure-aware allocation of reasoning computation. They do not establish that shorter reasoning is always better; the initial length finding is an association.
icml-2026-what-characterizes-effective-r.tldr: The fraction of reasoning spent on abandoned branches predicts correctness better than length or review frequency and guides interventions that improve accuracy.

paragraphs: Diffusion world models repeatedly refine representations to simulate evolving worlds, making inference costly. Reusing intermediate features can save computation, but the paper finds that caching policies from single-modality diffusion transfer poorly. Tokens differ across modalities and spatial locations, and a small number of difficult tokens can drive error growth over time.

WorldCache estimates token predictability using a physics-grounded curvature score. For tokens whose behavior changes direction abruptly, it applies a damped predictor guided by Hermite interpolation. A separate adaptive skipping mechanism accumulates a curvature-normalized drift signal and triggers recomputation when the difficult tokens begin to drift. This makes reuse sensitive to the tokens that constrain simulation stability.

Experiments report end-to-end speedups of up to 3.7 times while maintaining 98% of rollout quality. The results support adapting caching to heterogeneous token behavior and uneven temporal dynamics, rather than applying a uniform skipping schedule. The method offers inference acceleration without additional training, with the reported quality retention indicating a small measured trade-off rather than exact preservation of every rollout.
icml-2026-worldcache-accelerating-world-.tldr: WorldCache adapts feature reuse to token predictability and drift, delivering up to 3.7× reported speedup while maintaining 98% rollout quality.
